Rostrum: This is the front-most part that connects to the space behind your eyes (orbital regions of your frontal lobe). Genu: Sitting behind the rostrum, the genu

Cleveland Clinic  
Show all  
Rostrum & Genu (The Front)  
The Rostrum and Genu are the specific anterior (front) sections of the corpus callosum. They act as the dedicated data cables for the Frontal Lobes, connecting the left and right sides of the brain's "CEO."  
Because they connect the Prefrontal Cortex, these two structures are vital for executive function, emotional regulation, and social intelligence. If the posterior (Splenium) is for seeing the world, the anterior (Rostrum/Genu) is for navigating it socially and strategically.   
neurology icon  
Anatomy & Functions  
   
Genu ("The Knee"): The thick, curved bend at the front. It connects the Medial & Lateral Prefrontal Cortex.  
Rostrum ("The Beak"): The thin, beak-like extension below the Genu. It connects the Orbitofrontal Cortex (just behind the eyes).  
Anatomical diagram of the Corpus Callosum showing the Genu and Rostrum  
hub icon  
The Forceps Minor  
The nerve fibers exiting the Genu do not just stop; they curve forward into the frontal lobes, creating a U-shaped tract known as the Forceps Minor (or Anterior Forceps). This specific bundle is the physical hardware for the "Social Brain."   
Theory of Mind: The ability to understand that others have thoughts different from your own. Damage here can make it difficult to "read the room."  
Processing Speed: The density of these fibers correlates directly with how quickly you can make decisions and switch tasks.   
person\_off icon  
Specific Impact of Damage  
   
Because these areas connect the emotional and executive centers, damage to the Rostrum or Genu (or Agenesis) often presents as social and behavioral challenges rather than physical paralysis.   
Social Immaturity: Difficulty understanding sarcasm, humor, or social cues.  
Lack of Self-Awareness: Inability to reflect on one's own behavior or emotional state (poor insight).  
Confabulation: The brain may invent logical-sounding (but false) reasons for actions to bridge the gap between impulse and intent.
